question: Top 10 Women's Leadership Networks for 2028
body:
# Top 10 Women's Leadership Networks for 2028

![Women leaders collaborating at a leadership summit](https://images.pexels.com/photos/3184291/pexels-photo-3184291.jpeg)

## Direct Answer

The top 10 women's leadership networks for 2028 are **Chief**, **Ellevate Network**, **Lean In**, **Watermark**, **The Wing's successor collectives**, **Ellevest's leadership arm**, **Dreamers & Doers**, **Women in Revenue**, **The 3% Movement**, and **Athena Alliance**. Ranked below by the metric that actually matters for a working operator — not headcount, but *density of decision-makers per member and the concrete career leverage each connection produces* — these networks separate themselves in 2028 by moving past "community for community's sake" and toward measurable outcomes: board seats filled, comp negotiated, pipelines built, and P&L ownership won.

If you have thirty seconds and one budget line, the short version is this: **Chief** wins on executive density (VP-and-above only), **Women in Revenue** wins for anyone in a go-to-market or RevOps seat, and **Ellevate** wins on breadth if you want the widest net across industries and career stages. Everything else on this list earns its rank by doing one thing exceptionally well rather than everything adequately. Below, each network gets its own section explaining who it's for, what it costs in time and money, and the specific move that makes it worth joining in 2028.

The ranking logic is deliberate. A network with 500,000 members but no path to the room where offers get made is worth less to your career than a 4,000-person network where half the members can hire you, fund you, or refer you into a board search. We weighted for that. Here's how the ten stack up before the deep dive.

## 1. Chief

Chief remains the highest-leverage women's leadership network heading into 2028 because it solved the single hardest problem in professional community: **membership curation that actually holds a line.** Every member is a VP, SVP, C-suite executive, or founder of a funded company, and that gatekeeping is the entire product. When you walk into a Chief Core Group — the facilitated peer cohort of ten to twelve executives that anchors the membership — you are in a room where every person has hiring authority, board exposure, or budget ownership. That density is why a single warm introduction inside Chief can be worth more than a thousand LinkedIn connections outside it.

What earns Chief the top slot for 2028 specifically is how it has evolved past the pandemic-era "digital clubhouse" phase into a structured career-advancement engine. The network now pairs its Core Groups with executive coaching, a board-readiness track that has placed hundreds of women into their first directorships, and a private jobs channel where recruiters post C-suite roles before they hit the open market. The cost is real — annual dues run in the low thousands and there's a waitlist — but for a woman already operating at the director-to-VP threshold, Chief is the clearest paid accelerant to the next title. The one caveat: it is *not* for early-career professionals. If you're three years out of school, you'll be under-leveled and under-served; come back when you own a number or a team.

## 2. Ellevate Network

Ellevate takes the number two position by being the most *complete* network on the list — the one you'd recommend to someone who could only ever join one thing. Where Chief optimizes for the top of the pyramid, Ellevate spans the whole structure: individual contributors, managers, directors, and executives all coexist inside a global membership that stretches across finance, tech, healthcare, and the public sector. That breadth is a feature, not a compromise, because career mobility in 2028 increasingly moves *sideways* across industries, and Ellevate's cross-sector reach means the connection who helps you pivot from SaaS sales into fintech leadership is already inside the tent.

The 2028 version of Ellevate leans hard into programming that produces measurable skill gains rather than vibes. Its Squads — small, facilitated accountability groups that meet over a fixed number of weeks — have become the network's signature, giving members a structured push toward a specific goal (a raise, a launch, a job change) with peer pressure baked in. Ellevate also runs one of the most substantive editorial and event operations in the space, and its partnerships with employers mean some members get access through a corporate seat rather than personal dues. If Chief is the executive country club, Ellevate is the well-run public university: broader, more affordable, and genuinely transformative if you use it deliberately instead of passively.

![Professional women networking at a career development event](https://images.pexels.com/photos/3183197/pexels-photo-3183197.jpeg)

## 3. Lean In

Lean In earns the third slot on sheer scale and cultural staying power. Built around Sheryl Sandberg's framework and sustained by a global infrastructure of peer **Circles** — small groups of eight to twelve women who meet regularly to support one another's ambitions — Lean In is the closest thing the women's leadership space has to public infrastructure. In 2028 there are Circles on nearly every continent, inside thousands of companies, and across dozens of affinity communities (Lean In Latinas, Lean In Black Women, and more), which makes it the most *accessible* entry point on this entire list. There is no gatekeeping and no steep dues; you can start a Circle this week with a group text and the freely published facilitation guides.

The knock on Lean In has always been that scale dilutes intensity, and that's fair — a self-organized Circle is only as good as the women who show up to it. But that's also its genius: it externalizes the network-building to you and gives you a proven operating system to run it. For 2028, Lean In's most valuable asset is its research arm, particularly the annual *Women in the Workplace* study it produces with McKinsey, which remains the definitive dataset on the corporate pipeline and a rhetorical weapon you can bring into any DEI or promotion conversation. Join Lean In not for exclusive access but for a free, durable framework and a mountain of credible data to back your case.

## 4. Watermark

Watermark ranks fourth as the strongest *regional powerhouse* making a national play in 2028. Rooted in the San Francisco Bay Area and Silicon Valley, Watermark has spent years building the deepest bench of women executives, board directors, and founders in the technology corridor — and its geographic concentration is precisely what gives it teeth. Its board-placement programming, in particular, has a track record that most national networks can't match, because the boards doing the hiring and the women getting placed are often in the same zip code, attending the same Watermark conference.

What lifts Watermark for 2028 is that its flagship annual conference has grown into one of the most respected gatherings in the space, drawing keynote-caliber operators and creating the kind of high-density hallway conversations where real opportunities surface. Membership tiers give you access to executive circles, leadership development intensives, and a board-director pipeline that treats "get women into governance" as an operational goal with numbers attached, not a slogan. If you work in or near tech and you're aiming at a board seat within three years, Watermark should be at the top of your consideration set — it punches far above its regional weight and is expanding its virtual programming to reach members well beyond the Bay.

## 5. The Wing Collectives

The Wing itself famously flamed out, but its DNA scattered into a constellation of member-run women's collectives and coworking-plus-community spaces that, taken together, earn the number five slot for 2028. This entry is a category as much as a single brand: the successor networks that inherited The Wing's original insight — that women benefit from *physical, design-forward third spaces* built for their professional lives — while shedding the venture-backed overreach that sank the original. In 2028 these collectives operate leaner, are frequently member-owned or cooperatively governed, and cluster in major metros where in-person density still matters.

The reason this category makes the list is that hybrid and remote work has, paradoxically, *increased* the premium on intentional in-person gathering. A woman leading a distributed team in 2028 often has no default office and no built-in colleague network, and these collectives fill exactly that gap — a place to take a meeting, host a panel, or simply be around other ambitious women on a Tuesday afternoon. The trade-off is fragmentation: there's no single national membership, so the value is intensely local and you have to vet your city's specific collective. Where a strong one exists, though, it becomes the physical anchor that every purely-digital network on this list lacks.

## 6. Ellevest Leadership

Ellevest built its name as a women-focused investing platform, and its leadership and community arm ranks sixth in 2028 because it does something no purely social network attempts: it wires **professional advancement directly to financial power.** The premise is that leadership without wealth is fragile, and that a woman's negotiating leverage — her ability to walk away, to take a risk, to fund her own venture — is downstream of her balance sheet. Ellevest's community programming pairs career-development content with concrete financial education on equity compensation, negotiation, and wealth-building, closing a gap most leadership networks pretend doesn't exist.

For 2028, this integration is more relevant than ever as equity-heavy compensation packages and founder economics become central to how senior women actually accumulate power. Ellevest's members get frameworks for evaluating a startup offer, understanding a cap table, and negotiating not just salary but the full package — the kind of literacy that separates women who *hold* leadership from women who merely occupy the title. It ranks below the pure-play networks only because its community layer is secondary to its financial product, meaning the peer-connection density is thinner than Chief or Ellevate. But for a woman who suspects her real ceiling is financial rather than social, it's the most clarifying network on this list.

## 7. Dreamers & Doers

Dreamers & Doers claims the seventh slot as the premier network for **women founders and entrepreneurial operators** in 2028. Where most networks on this list serve women climbing corporate ladders, Dreamers & Doers is built for women who left the ladder to build their own thing — founders, indie operators, creators, and the growing class of "portfolio" professionals who run several ventures at once. Its curated, application-based membership emphasizes press amplification, warm introductions, and a genuinely useful digital collective where members trade tactical help on fundraising, hiring, and growth.

The reason it ranks this high is that entrepreneurship among women is one of the fastest-growing segments of economic activity heading into 2028, and the support infrastructure for it remains thin relative to corporate-leadership resources. Dreamers & Doers fills that gap with a network engineered specifically for the founder's problems: how to get covered, how to get funded, how to get in front of the right operator when you're a team of one. The community's collaborative "give-first" culture is its differentiator — members are expected to contribute introductions and expertise, not just extract them — which keeps the signal high. If you're building rather than climbing, this belongs near the top of your list despite its mid-pack overall rank.

## 8. Women in Revenue

Women in Revenue is the highest-ranked *function-specific* network on this list, and for anyone in a go-to-market, sales, RevOps, marketing, or customer-success leadership seat, it is arguably the most valuable network here full stop. It earns the eighth overall slot by owning a lane that the broad networks can't serve with any depth: the specific, brutal, number-carrying reality of revenue leadership. When a VP of Sales inside Women in Revenue talks about quota-setting, territory design, or the politics of a comp-plan overhaul, she's talking to peers who live the exact same fires — a level of tactical relevance that a general leadership network simply cannot provide.

For 2028, Women in Revenue matters more than its rank suggests because revenue leadership remains one of the most direct paths to the C-suite — the CRO-to-CEO pipeline is real, and it is disproportionately male at the top. The network's mentorship matching, salary and equity transparency resources, and events aimed squarely at moving women from individual-contributor selling into revenue *leadership* attack that imbalance at its source. If your career runs through a quota, this is your network; the general-purpose options above it are broader but will never speak your language this fluently. It's the strongest RevOps-adjacent community in the space, and on the PULSE audience specifically, it's the one we'd tell most readers to join first.

## 9. The 3% Movement

The 3% Movement earns the ninth position as the sharpest *industry-transformation* network in the leadership space, born from a single galvanizing statistic — the tiny share of creative directors in advertising who were women — and grown into a broad coalition pushing for equity in creative and marketing leadership. It ranks here because it demonstrates the model that the most effective 2028 networks share: a specific, measurable injustice as the organizing principle, and a community built to close that exact gap rather than to generically "empower."

What makes The 3% Movement worth a slot is that it operates simultaneously as a professional community and as an industry-reform engine, running conferences, certification and training programs, and employer accountability initiatives that change the hiring math from the top down. For women in advertising, marketing, design, and adjacent creative fields, it offers both peer connection and a credible institutional lever to pull when they hit a bias wall. It ranks below the function-specific Women in Revenue only because its industry footprint is narrower, but within that footprint its cultural influence is outsized. It's the model example of a network that treats a number on a slide as a mission to be operationalized.

## 10. Athena Alliance

Athena Alliance closes out the top ten as the network built around a single, high-stakes destination: **the boardroom.** Athena is a digital-first learning and leadership platform explicitly engineered to move senior women into board seats and C-suite roles, and it ranks tenth not because it's the least valuable but because it's the most *specialized* — a precision instrument for a specific ascent rather than a general community. If your explicit next goal is a board directorship or a C-level appointment, Athena's programming is aimed directly at that target.

The 2028 case for Athena is that board diversity mandates, investor pressure, and governance-transparency expectations have made "get qualified women into the boardroom" a live, funded priority across public and private companies alike — and Athena has positioned itself as the pipeline. Its members get executive coaching, board-readiness curriculum, salon-style peer learning with sitting directors, and access to a network of the people who actually sit on nominating committees. It's a paid, curated, outcome-oriented membership for women already near the top who want a structured runway into governance. As the tenth entry, it's the reminder that the best network for *you* depends entirely on the specific room you're trying to enter next.

## FAQ

**What is the best women's leadership network for 2028?** For pure executive density and access to hiring decision-makers, Chief ranks first. But "best" depends on your seat: Women in Revenue is best for go-to-market and RevOps leaders, Ellevate is best for the broadest cross-industry reach, and Athena Alliance is best if a board seat is your specific next goal. Match the network to the room you're trying to enter next, not to a headcount.

**Are paid women's leadership networks worth the money?** For anyone at the director level or above, yes — a single warm introduction to a hiring executive or board-search lead typically returns the annual dues many times over. Below that level, start with free options like Lean In Circles or an employer-sponsored Ellevate seat, and upgrade to a paid network like Chief once you own a team, a number, or a P&L that makes the higher-tier rooms relevant to you.

**How is Chief different from Ellevate Network?** Chief is executive-only (VP and above) and optimizes for depth — small facilitated peer groups of senior decision-makers plus a board-readiness track. Ellevate spans all career stages across many industries and optimizes for breadth and structured skill-building through its Squads. Chief is the executive country club; Ellevate is the well-run public university. Choose based on whether you need concentrated access at the top or a wider net across levels and sectors.

**Which network is best for women in sales or RevOps?** Women in Revenue, without close competition. It's built specifically for go-to-market leaders and speaks the language of quota, territory, comp plans, and the CRO track that general leadership networks can't match. It's the single most relevant network for anyone whose career runs through a revenue number, and the top recommendation for most PULSE readers in a go-to-market seat.

**Can I join a women's leadership network for free?** Yes. Lean In is the leading free option — you can start or join a Circle using freely published facilitation guides with no dues and no gatekeeping. Many employers also sponsor corporate seats in networks like Ellevate, so ask your manager or DEI lead whether a membership can be expensed before paying out of pocket for a premium network.

**Which women's leadership network helps most with getting a board seat?** Athena Alliance and Watermark both specialize in board placement, with structured board-readiness curriculum and direct access to nominating-committee-level connections. Chief also runs a strong board track as part of its broader membership. If a directorship is your explicit next goal, prioritize one of these three over a general-purpose community, since board placement is a specific skill and pipeline rather than a byproduct of networking.

**Do women's leadership networks actually improve career outcomes?** The measurable ones do. Networks that tie membership to concrete outcomes — board seats filled, comp negotiated, promotions won — produce results, while purely social communities produce mostly goodwill. The differentiator is whether the network has decision-makers in the room and a structured path to reach them. Judge any network by its density of people who can hire, fund, or refer you, not by its total membership count.
